item.title: Creating a Product Demo with SeleniumBase
item.description:
Selenium, as the most popular open-source web Test Automation framework today, has been developed for 20 years. It is powerful, and its webdriver protocol has also become a de facto standard in the field of Test Automation. Based on the Selenium framework, many extension frameworks built on top of it have emerged. One example is SeleniumBase, which we introduce in this article.

What Is SeleniumBase?

SeleniumBase is a Python library built on top of the Selenium framework that further enhances scripting. On top of Selenium’s original functionality, it simplifies the way automation scripts are written and invoked, and it is deeply integrated with the pytest framework. Most importantly, it provides a variety of different script modes, including script recording, slowed-down execution, in-run debugging, and the demo feature we are going to introduce in this article.

Although SeleniumBase is very powerful, the underlying implementation logic of the automation still follows the main characteristics of Selenium. So here we will not specifically introduce SeleniumBase’s wrappers for writing automation scripts. But one excellent thing about this library is that, through JS injection, it makes the automation running process more intuitive and easier to demonstrate.

For example, the demo creation we will see below.

Advantages of Completing a Demo Through Automation Scripts

As test engineers, especially with the popularity of agile development nowadays, the end of an iteration usually includes an iteration review and demo session. And as test engineers, a lot of the feature demos within iterations are done by us.

This also includes the fact that, when introducing product features to customers or leaders, explaining the features through actual product operations is essential as well.

But in practice, if we can display in advance the key points that need to be explained while the automated test is executing, the effect is very good, and it can also avoid some accidental misoperations on the spot.

So this feature of SeleniumBase can really play to its strengths here.

The Process of Creating a Product Demo with SeleniumBase

First, take a look at a demo of the open-source update information on my blog site, completed with SeleniumBase

In fact, its principle is fairly simple: through its wrapped BaseCase class, while the corresponding operation steps are being executed, it injects pre-packaged JS to highlight the elements being operated on and give some guidance hints.

The corresponding create_introjs_tour() method in the base class creates the demo tour. It also offers different JS theme choices here, which is very powerful.

Then add_tour_step() adds the steps, and play_tour() executes the steps.

from seleniumbase import BaseCase
BaseCase.main(__name__, __file__)


class MyTourClass(BaseCase):
 def test_blog_tour(self):
 self.open("https://chengxiaqiucao.github.io/")
 self.wait_for_element('[class="site-logo"]')

 self.set_introjs_colors("#f34565", "#c55409")
 self.create_introjs_tour() #
 self.add_tour_step("Selenium Base制作Demo演示", title="城下秋草的Demo")
 self.add_tour_step("查看热门开源项目", '#main-menu > li:nth-child(6) > a')
 self.play_tour()
 self.highlight_click('#main-menu > li:nth-child(6) > a')
 self.wait_for_element('[class="article-title"]')

 self.create_introjs_tour()
 self.add_tour_step("选择Selenium项目查看", '#seleniumpageselenium-10 > a')
 self.play_tour()
 self.highlight_click('#seleniumpageselenium-10 > a')
 self.ad_block()
 self.wait_for_element('[class="section-title"]')

 self.create_introjs_tour()
 self.add_tour_step("返回主页", '[class="site-logo"]')
 self.play_tour()
 self.highlight_click('[class="site-logo"]')
 self.wait_for_element('[title="搜索"]')

 self.create_introjs_tour()
 self.add_tour_step("3秒停顿后继续...")
 self.add_tour_step("开始下一个演示:")
 self.play_tour(interval=3)

As for the JS injected in the actual demo, we can also export the corresponding JS script through the self.export_tour statement, so that it can be used directly later.

Similarly, there is also its Demo mode, which is actually quite similar to the guided tour mode, except that it more often automatically slows down and highlights the automation execution steps to emphasize the verification points.

The above is my sharing on this cool feature of the SeleniumBase library~

item.title: Detailed Guide to Using Selenium Manager
item.description:
Selenium was born in 2004. With its open source nature and comprehensive features, it has long ranked Top1 in the field of Web test automation tools, and is currently the most mainstream Web test automation tool. Moreover, Selenium’s core Webdriver serves as the prevailing W3C standard and is widely referenced by various tools. It can be said to be the de facto standard for web test automation today.

Changes Brought by Selenium 4

After years of evolution, Selenium itself has now been released up to version V4.24. Although usages and materials related to the V3 version are still widely circulated online, Selenium 4 is actually a very major update. Several of its core components have undergone extensive refactoring.

  • WebDriver switched from the original Json Wire Protocol to the W3C standard definition
  • Selenium IDE completed its refactoring and feature optimization
  • Selenium Grid completed its refactoring and supports a more flexible cloud service architecture

In addition, Selenium 4 introduced a very important tool, which is the Selenium Manager we are going to focus on in this article (it was actually introduced only in V4.6, and its features were basically complete only by V4.12

Problems Caused by the Original Browser Driver Approach

To understand Selenium Manager, we still need to first understand how Selenium works.

How Selenium Works

The figure below is the basic architecture of Selenium’s local execution given on the official site.

As can be seen, Selenium actually accomplishes automation by driving different types of browsers (Chrome, Firefox, IE, Edge, Safari, etc.) through the webdriver protocol to complete specified actions, thereby achieving the goal of automated execution.

The key to driving a browser is the browser Driver that corresponds to the browser, such as ChromeDriver for Chrome, GecoDriver for FireFox, and so on.

And Selenium itself interacts with the browser Driver based on the WebDriver protocol.

The Problems It Causes

Although this architecture and working principle are clear, there is one problem: browser versions are constantly being updated. And the browser driver version needs to match the browser version; when mismatched driver and browser versions work together, various unexpected exceptions may occur. Therefore, for Selenium to work properly, before writing code with the Selenium library, the first thing is to ensure the deployment and matching of the browser driver and browser versions.

But browser versions and their corresponding drivers are usually maintained by the browser vendors.

So preparing the test automation environment here becomes rather complicated: you need to install the browser of the corresponding version under test, and at the same time find the driver corresponding to that version, then configure the relevant paths for Selenium, and only then can Selenium complete normal driving.

In addition, browser versions generally also have an auto-update feature. It may happen that, without the user noticing, the version has already changed, but at that time the driver version is not updated synchronously, so this also leads to the potential problem of driver and browser version mismatch.

This problem was actually not well resolved for a long time. With Selenium 3 and the early versions of Selenium 4, when we deployed a Selenium automation environment, obtaining and matching browser versions and driver versions was always a rather troublesome task, and because of this it discouraged quite a few test automation beginners.

Chrome’s Response to the Driver Problem

Since this problem has existed for a long time, browser vendors have also actually realized the troubles that a mismatch between driver and browser versions brings to test automation.

Taking Chrome as an example, if we go to the official ChromeDriver downloads page, we will see a page like this

As can be seen, Chrome Driver downloads here are only provided up to version 114, while the latest Chrome has actually already reached version 128. For versions after 115, the Chrome browser actually adjusted the driver release strategy, that is, Chrome driver is released in sync with the Chrome for Testing version, strictly ensuring the synchronous matching of driver and browser versions.

So why is there a Chrome for Testing version here?

As we mentioned earlier, browser versions have auto-update; if an auto-update happens, the driver version is not updated synchronously, thus causing a mismatch between driver and browser.

So the main difference between Chrome for Testing and the official version is actually that the for Testing version does not perform auto-updates.

In this way, together with the sharing of version numbers with the browser version, it is very convenient to ensure consistency between the browser and the driver.

Selenium’s Solution to the Driver Matching Problem

The above is the solution given by browsers to the driver matching problem, but it still does not completely solve the problem that the browser and Driver need to be obtained and specified separately. So Selenium’s official solution to this problem is Selenium Manager. It is actually an executable program included in the Selenium library, requiring no additional installation.

If we currently use Selenium V4 to execute a simple test automation script:

For example, to search for the Chinese phrase 城下秋草 测试 on Baidu, the code is as follows:

from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
from time import sleep

def test_baidu_search():
 option = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
 option.browser_version = '117'
 driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=option)

 driver.get("https://www.baidu.com")
 driver.find_element(By.ID,'kw').send_keys('城下秋草 测试')
 sleep(2)
 driver.find_element(By.ID,'su').click()
 sleep(3)
 driver.close()

As long as the Selenium library is installed, when executing, it can drive normally, without any special need to obtain the driver and configuration.

Source Code Analysis of Selenium 4 Launching Automation Execution

Here we analyze its startup process from Selenium’s Python source code:

driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=option)

This line of code actually calls the webdriver initialization code for the Chromium-based browser in the Selenium library, located at .venv/Lib/site-packages/selenium/webdriver/chromium/webdriver.py

During initialization, as can be seen, the DriverFinder method is used to obtain the paths of the browser and the Driver

def _run(args: List[str]) -> dict:
 """Executes the Selenium Manager Binary.

 :Args: - args: the components of the command being executed. :Returns: The log string containing the driver location. """ command = " ".join(args)
 logger.debug("Executing process: %s", command)
 try:
 if sys.platform == "win32":
 completed_proc = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, creationflags=subprocess.CREATE_NO_WINDOW)
 else:
 completed_proc = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True)
 stdout = completed_proc.stdout.decode("utf-8").rstrip("\n")
 stderr = completed_proc.stderr.decode("utf-8").rstrip("\n")
 output = json.loads(stdout) if stdout != "" else {"logs": [], "result": {}}
 except Exception as err:
 raise WebDriverException(f"Unsuccessful command executed: {command}") from err

 SeleniumManager._process_logs(output["logs"])
 result = output["result"]
 if completed_proc.returncode:
 raise WebDriverException(
 f"Unsuccessful command executed: {command}; code: {completed_proc.returncode}\n{result}\n{stderr}"
 )
 return result

Therefore, when the current Selenium 4 version executes, it uses the SeleniumManager program to determine the required browser and corresponding driver version.

The Selenium Manager Command-Line Program

Through SeleniumManager, based on the browser type and version we configure, it can automatically match the relevant driver version, and connect to the network on its own to obtain the files of the relevant driver and browser version for Selenium to call. For example, in the case above, we specified the browser version as 117; after execution, the downloaded browser and corresponding driver version are actually saved in the .cache\selenium directory under the user directory. The figure below shows the driver of version 117 currently updated by the execution.

selenium-manager 0.4.24
Selenium Manager is a CLI tool that automatically manages the browser/driver infrastructure required by Selenium.


Usage: selenium-manager [OPTIONS]
Options:
 --browser <BROWSER>
 Browser name (chrome, firefox, edge, iexplorer, safari, safaritp, or webview2)
 --driver <DRIVER>
 Driver name (chromedriver, geckodriver, msedgedriver, IEDriverServer, or safaridriver)
 --grid [<GRID_VERSION>]
 Selenium Grid. If version is not provided, the latest version is downloaded
 --driver-version <DRIVER_VERSION>
 Driver version (e.g., 106.0.5249.61, 0.31.0, etc.)
 --browser-version <BROWSER_VERSION>
 Major browser version (e.g., 105, 106, etc. Also: beta, dev, canary -or nightly-, and esr -in Firefox- are accepted)
 --browser-path <BROWSER_PATH>
 Browser path (absolute) for browser version detection (e.g., /usr/bin/google-chrome, "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome", "C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe")
 --driver-mirror-url <DRIVER_MIRROR_URL>
 Mirror for driver repositories (e.g., https://registry.npmmirror.com/-/binary/chromedriver/)
 --browser-mirror-url <BROWSER_MIRROR_URL>
 Mirror for browser repositories
 --output <OUTPUT>
 Output type: LOGGER (using INFO, WARN, etc.), JSON (custom JSON notation), SHELL (Unix-like), or MIXED (INFO, WARN, DEBUG, etc. to stderr and minimal JSON to stdout) [default: LOGGER]
 --os <OS>
 Operating system (i.e., windows, linux, or macos)
 --arch <ARCH>
 System architecture (i.e., x32, x64, or arm64)
 --proxy <PROXY>
 HTTP proxy for network connection (e.g., https://myproxy.net:8080)
 --timeout <TIMEOUT>
 Timeout for network requests (in seconds) [default: 300]
 --ttl <TTL>
 TTL (time-to-live) for discovered versions (online) of drivers and browsers [default: 3600]
 --cache-path <CACHE_PATH>
 Local folder used to store downloaded assets (drivers and browsers), local metadata, and configuration file [default: ~/.cache/selenium]
 --clear-cache
 Clear cache folder (~/.cache/selenium)
 --clear-metadata
 Clear metadata file (~/.cache/selenium/selenium-manager.json)
 --debug
 Display DEBUG messages
 --trace
 Display TRACE messages
 --log-level <LOG_LEVEL>
 Level for output messages. The possible values are: info, debug, trace, warn, error
 --offline
 Offline mode (i.e., disabling network requests and downloads)
 --force-browser-download
 Force to download browser (even when browser is already in the system)
 --avoid-browser-download
 Avoid to download browser (even when browser-version is specified)
 --language-binding <LANGUAGE_BINDING>
 Selenium language bindings that invokes Selenium Manager (e.g., Java, JavaScript, Python, DotNet, Ruby)
 --avoid-stats
 Avoid sends usage statistics to plausible.io
 -h, --help
 Print help
 -V, --version
 Print version
